Debt statistics: a holder’s median and a population’s average answer different questions

Read official Canadian debt-holding shares and conditional median balances with their confidence intervals, then explore an independent invented population that includes zero-debt units.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an independent invented population of exactly 100 family units

Interactive planning lab

Invented population: median including zero-debt units$0
Invented debt holders only: median$10,000
Invented population: mean including zero-debt units$4,000

The first two charts are fixed 2023 Survey of Financial Security observations for Canada, all ages, economic families and persons not in an economic family. Balance amounts are 2023 constant CAD. Published 95% confidence intervals are shown; they describe sampling uncertainty in the estimates, not the range of individual family debts. Categories overlap and are not additive. The last two charts and all metrics use a separate invented, unweighted population of exactly 100 family units, with every debt holder owing the same entered positive amount and everyone else owing zero. No source estimate initializes these controls. The toy population is not a reconstruction of the survey or a model of a reader’s household. Its mean is calculable because every individual value is specified; actual published medians and holding shares alone do not identify a population mean. With zero holders the conditional median is unavailable, rather than zero.

The central idea

Ask which units are included before comparing a debt balance. A median among borrowers excludes nonborrowers, and multiplying it by a holding share does not generally produce the population mean.

01

Ask whether the statistic describes everyone or only debt holders

A headline about how much debt families owe can conceal an important filtering step. Some statistics include all family units, while others describe only units that hold a particular debt. A dollar balance without its population definition can therefore be easy to misread.

The first two charts use Statistics Canada’s Survey of Financial Security table 11-10-0016-01. One measures the share holding each selected debt type. The other gives the median balance among holders of that debt, excluding units with no holding of it.

The reference population combines economic families with persons outside an economic family. It is not simply a count of individual adults or occupied dwellings. The 2023 survey covers the ten provinces and excludes Indigenous communities and collective dwellings. Its observations are context for understanding a population, rather than amounts a particular household ought to borrow.

02

Keep the holding share beside the holder-only balance

In 2023, the estimated holding shares were 39.0% for mortgage debt, 18.7% for lines of credit, 36.0% for credit-card and instalment debt, 12.0% for student loans and 27.1% for vehicle loans. Mortgage debt includes principal-residence mortgages and mortgages on other real estate.

The corresponding holder-only median balances were CAD 205,000, CAD 20,000, CAD 4,500, CAD 14,000 and CAD 20,000. These amounts use 2023 constant dollars. The survey reference year is 2023 and the release date is 29 October 2024; they are not current borrowing offers or a snapshot of today’s accounts.

A relatively common debt can have a comparatively small median balance among its holders. Conversely, a less common category can still matter greatly to the units that owe it. Neither the percentage alone nor the median alone supplies the full distribution of balances, interest rates or required payments.

The categories overlap. One family unit can have a mortgage, a vehicle loan and a credit-card balance. The holding shares are therefore not slices of one mutually exclusive pie and should not be added to find the share with any debt.

03

Read confidence intervals as uncertainty about an estimate

The official table supplies lower and upper 95% confidence bounds. The charts show them as whiskers and repeat both endpoints in the data tables. These are published survey intervals, rather than uncertainty ranges invented by this website.

For example, mortgage holding has an estimate of 39.0% with bounds of 38.0% and 39.9%. The holder-only mortgage median is CAD 205,000 with bounds of CAD 200,000 and CAD 215,000. The first interval concerns an estimated share; the second concerns an estimated median.

Neither means individual mortgage balances mostly fall between CAD 200,000 and CAD 215,000. A confidence interval around a summary statistic is different from the spread of people’s actual balances. The selected charts do not show percentiles or individual-level data.

Sampling, coverage and published rounding limit what can be concluded. The bars are descriptive; the page does not perform a significance test, infer a causal relationship between debt categories or place a reader at a national debt percentile.

04

Build a separate population where every value is known

The interactive illustration is independent of the survey. It creates exactly 100 unweighted family units. At the default, forty hold an invented debt balance of CAD 10,000 each and sixty owe zero of that debt. Neither control starts from an official observation.

The median among the forty positive-debt units is CAD 10,000 because every one owes that amount. The median across all 100 units is zero: after sorting all balances, both the fiftieth and fifty-first observations are zero.

The population mean is different again. Total debt is forty times CAD 10,000, or CAD 400,000. Dividing by 100 gives CAD 4,000 per invented family unit. This is an average over everyone, including the sixty zero balances.

All three results are internally consistent. They answer different questions about an explicitly specified dataset. The example does not imply that real borrowers have equal debts or that the actual survey can be reconstructed from one percentage and one median.

05

Watch the median respond differently when more units hold debt

The final chart changes the whole number of holders from zero to one hundred while retaining the selected positive balance. Every point represents a different invented population, not the same families moving through time.

With fewer than fifty holders, both middle observations in this particular population remain zero. At exactly fifty holders, the ordinary even-sample median averages a zero balance and a CAD 10,000 balance, producing CAD 5,000. At fifty-one holders, both middle observations are CAD 10,000.

The mean rises gradually with the holder count because total debt rises by the same amount for each added identical borrower. The holder-only median stays CAD 10,000 whenever at least one holder exists. With no holders, that conditional median is unavailable; assigning it zero would hide the empty subset.

This unweighted teaching rule is not a reproduction of the survey’s weighting or estimation procedure. It isolates the effect of including zero balances before interpreting a summary statistic.

06

Use population context without turning a median into a personal limit

In the invented population, multiplying the holder share by the identical holder balance gives the all-unit mean because every positive balance is known and equal. That shortcut does not generally work with a real conditional median. The population mean requires the conditional mean, alongside the holding share, rather than the middle holder’s balance.

Likewise, adding several holder-only medians does not create the debt of one typical family. Each category can describe a different subset, and medians do not generally add even when measurements come from the same population.

For a household plan, list its actual balances, contractual rates, payment amounts and due dates. Consider available cash and repayment capacity separately from national comparisons. The official charts clarify who and what was measured; the independent illustration makes the arithmetic consequences of changing that denominator visible.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Two fixed charts use 2023 Survey of Financial Security estimates and published 95% confidence bounds, checked against the original CSV. Two independent hypothetical charts use exactly 100 invented family units with identical positive balances among holders. They do not reconstruct the survey or rank a reader. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 11-10-0016-01, Survey of Financial Security ↗

    2023, Canada, all ages, economic families and persons not in an economic family; released 29 October 2024 and checked 25 October 2026. Five holding shares, five holder-only medians and all twenty published confidence-bound cells are verified against the original CSV. Balances use 2023 constant CAD. Nonzero holdings define the debt subsets.

  2. Statistics Canada · Survey of Financial Security, 2023 release ↗

    Used for survey reference year, publication date, family-unit definition, ten-province coverage and sampling limitations. The 100-unit population is independent original arithmetic, with no survey weighting or claim to reproduce observed debt distributions.
